title: 07 — Databricks Platform
html:
07 — Databricks Platform

The one idea: Databricks is managed Spark plus everything a team needs around it — a governed catalog, several kinds of compute, declarative pipelines, orchestration, SQL warehouses and ML tooling — all operating on open Delta tables that live in your cloud storage. You pay for compute by the DBU; your data stays in your account.

1. What Databricks is

Databricks is a data and AI platform built by the original creators of Apache Spark. It runs on Azure (as the first-party service Azure Databricks), AWS and Google Cloud.

Its main components, in the order you usually meet them:

Area What it gives you
Workspace The UI and API surface: notebooks, files, Git folders, jobs, SQL editor, dashboards
Compute Spark clusters, serverless compute, SQL warehouses
Delta Lake The default table format (see chapter 08)
Unity Catalog Governance: catalog, permissions, lineage, auditing
Lakeflow Data engineering tooling: Lakeflow Connect (managed ingestion connectors), Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines (formerly Delta Live Tables), Lakeflow Jobs (formerly Workflows)
Databricks SQL SQL warehouses, SQL editor, dashboards, alerts
ML / AI MLflow, feature engineering, model serving, vector search

2. Control plane vs compute plane

---
title: Databricks architecture — control plane and compute plane
---
flowchart TB
    U["Users, CI/CD, BI tools"] --> CP
    subgraph CP["Control plane (Databricks-managed account)"]
        WA["Web app and REST APIs"]
        JS["Job scheduler"]
        UC["Unity Catalog service"]
        NB["Notebook and workspace metadata"]
    end
    subgraph CUST["Your cloud subscription"]
        subgraph CL["Classic compute plane"]
            DR["Cluster driver and workers<br/>(VMs in your VNet)"]
        end
        ST[("Your storage<br/>ADLS Gen2 / S3")]
    end
    subgraph SL["Serverless compute plane (Databricks-managed)"]
        SV["Serverless jobs, notebooks,<br/>SQL warehouses, pipelines"]
    end
    CP -->|"launch and manage"| CL
    CP -->|"launch and manage"| SL
    DR <--> ST
    SV <-->|"via governed credentials"| ST
Plane Where it runs What it contains
Control plane Databricks' cloud account Web UI, APIs, job scheduler, notebook source, cluster management, Unity Catalog metadata service
Classic compute plane Your cloud subscription, in a VNet (Databricks-managed or your own via VNet injection) Cluster VMs that process your data
Serverless compute plane Databricks' cloud account, isolated per workspace Compute that starts in seconds and is fully managed

Your data sits in your own storage accounts in both cases. With classic compute, the VMs also run in your subscription (and you see the VM charges from your cloud provider); with serverless, Databricks runs the machines and bundles the infrastructure cost into the DBU price.

3. Workspace, notebooks and Git folders

  • Workspace: a deployment of Databricks with its own URL, users, notebooks and compute. Organisations usually have separate workspaces per environment (dev/test/prod) or per business unit, all attached to the same Unity Catalog metastore in a region.
  • Notebooks: cells of Python, SQL, Scala or R, with magic commands (%sql, %python, %md, %run, %pip). Good for exploration and for running production code, but production logic is better kept in modules that are imported and tested.
  • Git folders (formerly Repos): clone a Git repository into the workspace, work on branches, commit and push from the UI. Notebooks are stored as source files so diffs are readable.
  • Workspace files: arbitrary files (Python modules, config, small data) alongside notebooks, importable from notebooks.
  • Secrets: secret scopes (Databricks-backed or backed by Azure Key Vault) accessed with dbutils.secrets.get(scope, key); values are redacted in notebook output.

4. Compute types and the cost model

Compute What it is Starts Best for Billing notes
All-purpose (interactive) cluster A cluster you create and share for notebook work Minutes Development, exploration Highest DBU rate; keep auto-termination short
Job compute A cluster created for one job run and terminated after Minutes Scheduled production pipelines on classic compute Much lower DBU rate than all-purpose
Serverless compute for notebooks and jobs Databricks-managed compute, no cluster config Seconds Jobs and notebooks without infrastructure tuning DBU includes the infrastructure; no idle VMs to pay for
SQL warehouse (classic / pro / serverless) Compute for SQL queries and BI, Photon enabled Serverless: seconds; classic/pro: minutes Dashboards, BI tools, analysts, dbt SQL Sized by T-shirt size; scales with concurrency; auto-stop
Pipeline compute Clusters or serverless running Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines Varies Declarative pipelines Priced by pipeline edition/tier

DBUs

A DBU (Databricks Unit) is a normalised unit of processing capacity per hour, metered per second. What you pay is roughly:

Classic compute cost  = (DBUs consumed × DBU rate for that compute type and tier) + cloud VM cost
Serverless cost       = DBUs consumed × serverless DBU rate (infrastructure included)

The DBU rate varies by compute type (all-purpose is dearer than jobs), by pricing tier, and by features like Photon. Exact prices change and differ by cloud and region, so check the current price list rather than memorising numbers.

Cost habits that matter:

  • Run production on job compute or serverless, never on all-purpose clusters.
  • Set auto-termination on interactive clusters (e.g. 20–30 minutes).
  • Use cluster policies to cap sizes and enforce tags.
  • Tag compute with cost centre/team and use the system tables (system.billing.usage) to attribute spend.
  • Use spot instances for workers on fault-tolerant batch jobs (keep the driver on-demand).

Photon

Photon is Databricks' vectorised query engine written in C++. It executes supported Spark SQL and DataFrame operations natively instead of in the JVM, which speeds up scans, joins, aggregations and Delta writes (including MERGE). It is always on for SQL warehouses and serverless, and optional on classic clusters, where it raises the DBU rate. It helps most on SQL-heavy workloads with large scans and joins; it does not speed up Python UDFs or RDD code.

5. Unity Catalog

Unity Catalog (UC) is the governance layer: a single place to define data objects, grant access, audit use and track lineage across workspaces.

---
title: Unity Catalog object hierarchy
---
flowchart TB
    M["Metastore<br/>(one per region, attached to workspaces)"]
    M --> C1["Catalog: prod"]
    M --> C2["Catalog: dev"]
    M --> SC["Storage credentials and external locations"]
    C1 --> S1["Schema: silver"]
    C1 --> S2["Schema: gold"]
    S1 --> T1["Table: customers"]
    S1 --> V1["View: active_customers"]
    S1 --> VO["Volume: landing_files"]
    S2 --> T2["Materialized view: daily_revenue"]
    S2 --> F1["Function: mask_email"]
    S2 --> MD["Registered model: churn"]

The three-level namespace

Every object is addressed as catalog.schema.object:

SELECT * FROM prod.silver.customers;

USE CATALOG prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;
SELECT * FROM customers;

Common layouts: one catalog per environment (dev, test, prod) with schemas per layer or domain; or one catalog per domain with schemas per layer. Choose one and apply it consistently — it becomes the backbone of permissions.

Securable objects

Object Purpose
Metastore Top-level container, one per region; holds all catalogs
Catalog First level of the namespace; often an environment or domain
Schema Second level; a database-like grouping
Table Managed (UC controls storage location and lifecycle) or external (you control the location)
View / materialized view Saved queries; materialized views store results
Volume Governed access to non-tabular files (/Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/...)
Function SQL or Python UDFs, also used for row filters and column masks
Model MLflow registered models
Storage credential / external location How UC reaches cloud storage (e.g. an Azure managed identity) and which paths are allowed

Grants

Permissions are granted to users, groups or service principals and inherit downwards. To read a table a principal needs USE CATALOG on the catalog, USE SCHEMA on the schema and SELECT on the table.

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG prod TO `data-analysts`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA  ON SCHEMA  prod.gold TO `data-analysts`;
GRANT SELECT      ON SCHEMA  prod.gold TO `data-analysts`;   -- all current and future tables in the schema

GRANT MODIFY ON TABLE prod.silver.customers TO `svc-ingestion`;

-- Row filter: admins see everything, the EMEA sales group sees only EMEA rows
CREATE FUNCTION prod.gold.region_filter(row_region STRING)
RETURN is_account_group_member('admins')
    OR (is_account_group_member('emea-sales') AND row_region = 'EMEA');
ALTER TABLE prod.gold.sales SET ROW FILTER prod.gold.region_filter ON (region);

-- Column mask
CREATE FUNCTION prod.gold.mask_email(email STRING)
RETURN CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('pii-readers') THEN email ELSE '***' END;
ALTER TABLE prod.gold.customers ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK prod.gold.mask_email;

Grant to groups, never to individuals, and run production jobs as service principals.

Lineage and auditing

UC captures table- and column-level lineage automatically for queries run on UC-enabled compute, visible in Catalog Explorer and queryable via system tables. Audit logs record who accessed what. This is the backbone for impact analysis ("what breaks if I change this column?") and for compliance.

6. Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines (formerly Delta Live Tables)

A declarative pipeline lets you define what tables should exist and how each is derived; the framework works out dependencies, creates and updates tables, manages checkpoints and retries, and records data quality.

Two main dataset types:

Type Semantics Use for
Streaming table Incrementally processes each new input record once (append-style) Ingestion from files/Kafka, bronze and many silver tables, CDC targets
Materialized view Result of a query, kept up to date; refreshed incrementally where the engine can, otherwise recomputed Aggregations, joins, gold tables

(There are also plain views, used as intermediate steps without persisting data.)

import dlt   # newer runtimes also expose this as `from pyspark import pipelines as dp`
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

@dlt.table(comment="Raw orders from the landing volume")
def orders_bronze():
    return (spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")
            .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
            .load("/Volumes/prod/landing/orders/"))

@dlt.table(comment="Typed, validated orders")
@dlt.expect("valid_amount", "amount >= 0")                       # keep row, record violation
@dlt.expect_or_drop("has_order_id", "order_id IS NOT NULL")      # drop violating rows
@dlt.expect_or_fail("known_currency", "currency IN ('GBP','EUR','USD')")  # fail the update
def orders_silver():
    return (dlt.read_stream("orders_bronze")
            .select(
                F.col("order_id"),
                F.col("customer_id"),
                F.col("amount").cast("decimal(18,2)").alias("amount"),
                F.col("currency"),
                F.to_timestamp("order_ts").alias("order_ts")))

@dlt.table(comment="Daily revenue")
def daily_revenue_gold():
    return (dlt.read("orders_silver")
            .groupBy(F.to_date("order_ts").alias("order_date"), "currency")
            .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))

The same in SQL:

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE orders_bronze
AS SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files('/Volumes/prod/landing/orders/', format => 'json');

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE orders_silver (
  CONSTRAINT valid_amount   EXPECT (amount >= 0),
  CONSTRAINT has_order_id   EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW,
  CONSTRAINT known_currency EXPECT (currency IN ('GBP','EUR','USD')) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
)
AS SELECT order_id, customer_id, CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(18,2)) AS amount, currency,
          to_timestamp(order_ts) AS order_ts
   FROM STREAM(orders_bronze);

CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue_gold
AS SELECT to_date(order_ts) AS order_date, currency, SUM(amount) AS revenue
   FROM orders_silver
   GROUP BY to_date(order_ts), currency;

CDC into SCD1/SCD2

Declarative pipelines include a built-in API for applying a change feed to a target, handling out-of-order events by a sequencing column. It has been known as APPLY CHANGES INTO and more recently AUTO CDC:

dlt.create_streaming_table("customers_silver")

dlt.apply_changes(                 # newer name: create_auto_cdc_flow
    target="customers_silver",
    source="customers_cdc_bronze",
    keys=["customer_id"],
    sequence_by=F.col("change_ts"),
    apply_as_deletes=F.expr("op = 'DELETE'"),
    except_column_list=["op", "change_ts"],
    stored_as_scd_type=2)          # or 1

For SCD type 2 the framework adds __START_AT and __END_AT columns to the target.

Pipelines run in triggered mode (process available data, then stop) or continuous mode, and in development mode (reuse cluster, no retries) or production mode.

7. Auto Loader

Auto Loader is a Structured Streaming source (cloudFiles) for ingesting files incrementally from cloud storage.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

(spark.readStream
    .format("cloudFiles")
    .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "/Volumes/prod/meta/schemas/orders")
    .option("cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes", "true")
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "addNewColumns")
    .load("abfss://landing@mystorage.dfs.core.windows.net/orders/")
    .withColumn("_source_file", F.col("_metadata.file_path"))
    .withColumn("_ingested_at", F.current_timestamp())
    .writeStream
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/prod/meta/checkpoints/orders_bronze")
    .trigger(availableNow=True)
    .toTable("prod.bronze.orders"))

What it gives you over reading a folder yourself:

  • Exactly-once file tracking: discovered files are recorded in the checkpoint (a RocksDB store), so each file is processed once even across restarts.
  • Two discovery modes: directory listing (default, simple) and file notification (subscribes to storage events via queue services, scales to very large directories). Newer runtimes can use managed file events through Unity Catalog external locations.
  • Schema inference and evolution: infers the schema, stores it at schemaLocation, and handles new columns according to schemaEvolutionMode (addNewColumns stops the stream so it restarts with the new schema; rescue routes unexpected data to a rescued-data column; failOnNewColumns; none).
  • Rescued data column (_rescued_data): values that do not match the schema are kept as JSON rather than silently dropped.

8. Workflows (Lakeflow Jobs)

A job is the orchestration unit: a DAG of tasks with dependencies, triggers, parameters, retries, timeouts, notifications and a compute definition.

---
title: A typical Lakeflow Job
---
flowchart LR
    T1["ingest_orders<br/>(notebook)"] --> T3["silver_pipeline<br/>(declarative pipeline)"]
    T2["ingest_customers<br/>(Python wheel)"] --> T3
    T3 --> T4["gold_models<br/>(dbt / SQL task)"]
    T4 --> T5{"quality_gate<br/>(if/else task)"}
    T5 -->|"pass"| T6["refresh_dashboard"]
    T5 -->|"fail"| T7["notify_team"]

Task types include notebooks, Python scripts and wheels, SQL queries and files, declarative pipelines, dbt, JAR, other jobs (run-job task), if/else conditions and for-each loops.

Triggers: scheduled (cron), file arrival (when new files land in a UC location), table update (when upstream tables change, where supported), continuous, or manual/API.

Useful features: task values (pass small values between tasks), job parameters with dynamic values like {{job.start_time.iso_date}}, repair runs (rerun only failed tasks), per-task retries, and run-as service principals. Details on orchestration practice are in chapter 10.

9. Databricks Asset Bundles (CI/CD)

Asset Bundles (DABs) define jobs, pipelines, and other workspace resources as YAML alongside your code, and deploy them to target environments with the Databricks CLI.

# databricks.yml
bundle:
  name: orders_pipeline

include:
  - resources/*.yml

targets:
  dev:
    mode: development
    default: true
    workspace:
      host: https://adb-1111111111111111.11.azuredatabricks.net
  prod:
    mode: production
    workspace:
      host: https://adb-2222222222222222.22.azuredatabricks.net
    run_as:
      service_principal_name: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"

# resources/orders_job.yml
resources:
  jobs:
    orders_daily:
      name: orders_daily
      schedule:
        quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 2 * * ?"
        timezone_id: UTC
      tasks:
        - task_key: ingest
          notebook_task:
            notebook_path: ../src/ingest_orders.py
        - task_key: transform
          depends_on:
            - task_key: ingest
          python_wheel_task:
            package_name: orders
            entry_point: transform
          libraries:
            - whl: ../dist/*.whl

databricks bundle validate -t dev
databricks bundle deploy   -t dev
databricks bundle run      -t dev orders_daily
databricks bundle deploy   -t prod     # from CI, authenticated as a service principal

In development mode, resources are prefixed per user and schedules are paused, so several engineers can deploy the same bundle into one dev workspace without collisions.

10. MLflow

MLflow, managed in Databricks, covers:

  • Tracking: log parameters, metrics, artifacts and models per run; compare runs in the UI.
  • Models in Unity Catalog: register model versions under catalog.schema.model, with aliases (e.g. champion) and the same grants and lineage as tables.
  • Serving: deploy registered models to model serving endpoints, or use them for batch scoring in Spark.
  • GenAI features: tracing and evaluation for LLM applications.
import mlflow
mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")

with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_param("max_depth", 6)
    mlflow.log_metric("auc", 0.87)
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, "model",
                             registered_model_name="prod.ml.churn_model",
                             input_example=X_train.head(5))

11. Databricks SQL and dashboards

  • SQL warehouses serve SQL from the editor, dashboards, and external BI tools (Power BI, Tableau) over JDBC/ODBC.
  • SQL editor: write and schedule queries; results can drive alerts (notify when a condition is met).
  • Dashboards (AI/BI dashboards): build visualisations on warehouse queries and share them with workspace users.
  • Query history and query profile: the SQL-side equivalent of the Spark UI for diagnosing slow queries.

For Power BI, connect through the Azure Databricks connector to a SQL warehouse, prefer a star-schema gold layer, and consider DirectQuery for very large or fresh data, Import for smaller, performance-critical models.

12. Azure Databricks setup

---
title: Azure Databricks storage access with Unity Catalog
---
flowchart LR
    WS["Azure Databricks workspace"] --> UCM["Unity Catalog metastore"]
    UCM --> SCR["Storage credential"]
    SCR --> AC["Access Connector for Azure Databricks<br/>(managed identity)"]
    AC -->|"RBAC: Storage Blob Data Contributor"| ADLS[("ADLS Gen2 account")]
    UCM --> EL["External location<br/>abfss://container@account..."]
    EL --> SCR
  • Azure Databricks is a first-party Azure service: provision a workspace resource in a resource group; billing appears on your Azure invoice.
  • Storage: ADLS Gen2 with hierarchical namespace. Unity Catalog accesses it through an Access Connector for Azure Databricks, an Azure resource with a managed identity. You grant that identity RBAC on the storage account, register it as a storage credential, and define external locations for the paths UC may use.
  • Avoid account keys and mount points in new designs; UC external locations and volumes replace mounts.
  • Networking: VNet injection (deploy classic compute into your own VNet), secure cluster connectivity (no public IPs on cluster nodes), Private Link for front-end and back-end connectivity.
  • Identity: users and groups sync from Microsoft Entra ID (SCIM/automatic identity management); jobs run as Entra ID service principals.
  • Secrets: Azure Key Vault-backed secret scopes.

Azure / .NET mapping

Need Azure / .NET approach
Trigger a Databricks job from a .NET service Call the Jobs REST API (/api/2.1/jobs/run-now) with an Entra ID token for a service principal
Query gold tables from a .NET API Databricks SQL warehouse via ODBC/JDBC driver or the SQL Statement Execution REST API
Orchestrate from Azure Azure Data Factory's Databricks activities, or let Lakeflow Jobs own orchestration
CI/CD Asset Bundles run from GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines using workload identity federation for the service principal
Governance across Azure Unity Catalog for Databricks objects; Microsoft Purview for estate-wide cataloguing

Review checklist

  • I can explain control plane vs compute plane and where my data lives.
  • I know the compute types and which to use for development, production jobs and BI.
  • I can explain how DBUs translate to cost for classic vs serverless compute.
  • I know when Photon helps and when it does not.
  • I can navigate the Unity Catalog hierarchy and write grants for a reader group.
  • I can explain streaming tables vs materialized views and the three expectation behaviours.
  • I know what Auto Loader adds over reading a folder and how schema evolution works.
  • I can design a multi-task job with dependencies, retries and a file-arrival trigger.
  • I can deploy a job to dev and prod with Asset Bundles.
  • I can describe the Azure storage access chain: access connector → storage credential → external location.
